learningObjectives.title: A Shakespeare play studied in detail
Personal response in a controlled assessment task
The controlled assessment task and its requirements

questions.q: In the CCEA GCSE English Literature specification, how is Unit 3: The Study of Shakespeare assessed?
options: By a controlled assessment task
By a two-hour written examination
By a spoken presentation only
By an online multiple-choice test
questions.explain: Unit 3 is the Study of Shakespeare, assessed through a controlled assessment task rather than an external written exam.

questions.q: How is a candidate's Unit 3 controlled assessment response marked and quality-assured?
options: Marked within the centre and externally moderated by CCEA
Marked only by the candidate through self-assessment
Marked entirely in a sealed external examination
Not marked, as it is completed only for practice
questions.explain: Controlled assessment is internally marked by the centre and then externally moderated by the exam board to ensure consistency.

questions.q: For Unit 3, how many Shakespeare plays does a candidate study in detail?
options: One
Two
Three
Four
questions.explain: Candidates study a single Shakespeare play in detail as the basis for their controlled assessment response.

questions.q: What is 'iambic pentameter', the metre Shakespeare frequently uses?
options: A line of five iambic feet, giving ten syllables with alternating unstressed and stressed beats
A rhyming couplet of eight syllables
A line that must always rhyme with the next
A fourteen-line love poem
questions.explain: Iambic pentameter has five iambs per line, producing a ten-syllable rhythm of unstressed-stressed beats.

questions.q: What is a soliloquy?
options: A speech in which a character, alone on stage, reveals their thoughts to the audience
A conversation between two characters
A short comic scene between acts
A stage direction describing movement
questions.explain: A soliloquy is delivered by a character alone on stage, sharing private thoughts directly with the audience.

questions.q: What is dramatic irony?
options: When the audience knows something that a character on stage does not
When a character speaks in rhyming couplets
When two characters argue on stage
When a tragedy ends happily
questions.explain: Dramatic irony occurs when the audience possesses knowledge that a character lacks, creating tension.

questions.q: What is 'blank verse', widely used in Shakespeare's plays?
options: Unrhymed iambic pentameter
Rhyming couplets throughout
Prose written with no punctuation
A song performed by the chorus
questions.explain: Blank verse is unrhymed iambic pentameter, the flexible verse form used for much of Shakespeare's dialogue.

questions.q: To support a personal response, a candidate is expected to use which of the following?
options: Relevant textual references, including short quotations from the play
Only their own opinion with no reference to the text
A summary of the whole plot with no analysis
Quotations from other plays not being studied
questions.explain: A strong personal response is supported by precise textual references and well-chosen quotations from the play.

questions.q: Why might Shakespeare give a character a soliloquy?
options: To reveal the character's private thoughts, motives or inner conflict to the audience
To speed up the plot by skipping over scenes
To provide comic relief through wordplay only
To describe the setting through stage directions
questions.explain: Soliloquies let the audience access a character's inner thoughts, motives and conflicts that others cannot hear.

questions.q: What effect does dramatic irony typically create for an audience?
options: Tension or engagement, as the audience anticipates consequences the character cannot foresee
Confusion, because no one understands the plot
Rhythm, because it controls the metre of the lines
Rhyme, because it links the ends of lines
questions.explain: Because the audience knows more than the character, dramatic irony builds suspense and emotional engagement.

questions.q: In Shakespeare's plays, a shift from verse into prose can often signal which of the following?
options: A change such as lower social status, madness, or a comic or informal moment
That the play is about to end
That the actor has forgotten the lines
That the scene is set at night
questions.explain: Shakespeare often uses prose for lower-status characters, comic scenes, or moments of disorder such as madness.

questions.q: Why is understanding the context of a Shakespeare play valuable in a detailed study?
options: It helps explain how the play's ideas relate to the beliefs and society of the time it was written
It allows the candidate to avoid quoting the text
It replaces the need to analyse the language
It guarantees full marks regardless of the argument
questions.explain: Contextual understanding illuminates how a play's themes connect to the values and society of Shakespeare's era.

questions.q: Developing a 'critical style' in a personal response means doing what?
options: Analysing and evaluating the writer's choices rather than only retelling events
Criticising the play for being difficult to read
Writing only in the first person about personal feelings
Listing every character who appears in the play
questions.explain: A critical style analyses and evaluates the writer's methods and effects instead of simply narrating the plot.

questions.q: Why is the final written response produced under supervised, controlled conditions?
options: To ensure the work is authentically the candidate's own
To make the task considerably shorter
To allow candidates to answer in groups
To remove the need for any marking
questions.explain: Controlled conditions safeguard authenticity, confirming that the final response is genuinely the candidate's own work.

questions.q: Why might a playwright use an aside?
options: To let a character share a thought with the audience that other characters are not meant to hear
To end a scene with a rhyming couplet
To mark the interval between two acts
To describe the stage lighting
questions.explain: An aside briefly reveals a character's thoughts to the audience while other characters remain unaware.

questions.q: What does an 'informed personal response' involve?
options: A personal interpretation supported by understanding of, and evidence from, the text
A personal opinion unconnected to the text
A memorised model answer reproduced exactly
A factual biography of Shakespeare's life
questions.explain: An informed personal response combines the candidate's own interpretation with textual understanding and evidence.

questions.q: Which of these lines is written in iambic pentameter?
options: 'But soft, what light through yonder window breaks?'
'To be.'
'Now is the winter'
'Friends, Romans, countrymen'
questions.explain: This line has ten syllables arranged in five iambs, making it a clear example of iambic pentameter.

questions.q: A character stands alone on an empty stage and speaks aloud about their guilt and fear. This is best described as which of the following?
options: A soliloquy
An aside
A prologue
A stage direction
questions.explain: A character alone on stage voicing their inner thoughts is delivering a soliloquy.

questions.q: Which sentence best shows an informed personal response with an embedded quotation?
options: Macbeth's description of life as 'a walking shadow' suggests his growing sense of despair and futility.
Macbeth is a play written by Shakespeare about a king.
I did not really enjoy the play very much at all.
'A walking shadow.'
questions.explain: This response embeds a short quotation and interprets its effect, showing an informed personal response.

questions.q: The audience knows a character's drink is poisoned, but the character happily drinks it. This is an example of which technique?
options: Dramatic irony
Blank verse
A rhyming couplet
A soliloquy
questions.explain: The audience knowing about the poison while the character does not is a clear case of dramatic irony.

specSource: CCEA GCSE English Literature (2017) specification; Unit 3: The Study of Shakespeare (Controlled Assessment)
